idiom_name: sqlite3 spool table (WAL, synchronous=FULL) + daemon drain thread
implementation_notes: The standard library is enough: keep a spool table in an sqlite3 database, set PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL and PRAGMA synchronous=FULL so a committed INSERT is synced to disk (with NORMAL, WAL commits survive application crashes but not power loss), and treat commit() as the accept point. A daemon thread or an asyncio task selects pending rows, delivers them and deletes a row only after the peer acknowledged; a file spool using os.fsync() with os.replace() is the alternative when sqlite3 is unavailable. Broker clients such as Celery carry the message only once it reached the broker, so a sender-side spool in front of them is still yours to build - the classic structure is justified exactly in that gap.
code_sketch:
con = sqlite3.connect("spool.db", isolation_level=None)
con.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
con.execute("PRAGMA synchronous=FULL")     # the commit is the accept point
con.execute("INSERT INTO spool(payload, created) VALUES (?, ?)", (blob, time.time()))
# drainer thread, started at boot as well:
for row in con.execute("SELECT id, payload FROM spool ORDER BY id"):
    try: deliver(row["payload"]); con.execute("DELETE FROM spool WHERE id=?", (row["id"],))
    except OSError: time.sleep(backoff); break   # row stays for the next pass
pitfalls: synchronous=NORMAL is not power-loss durable in WAL mode: a machine crash rolls back accepted messages even though commit() returned.
A sqlite3 connection belongs to the thread that created it (check_same_thread); sharing one between sender and drainer without a lock raises or corrupts.
Daemon threads die silently at interpreter exit, so the spool stops draining while accepts continue - supervise the drainer or use a non-daemon thread with an explicit shutdown.
Deleting rows before the acknowledgement, or committing the business write and the spool row in separate transactions, re-creates the loss window.
